locations.name: Warwick
locations.depot: our Cornubia yard south of Brisbane, run west on the Cunningham Highway and over the Gap
locations.leadTime: Usually 3–5 business days from order to on the ground
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft on town and farm blocks; crane truck or side loader for 40ft and for anything lifted over a fence
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Warwick and the Southern Downs. Black soil, granite country, frost and the Cunninghams Gap run allowed for.
locations.line: Warwick sits at the top of a climb, and the climb is the first thing we think about. Every box we send there leaves Cornubia, runs west along the Cunningham and works its way up over the Gap, which is steep, tightly wound, fogged in most cold mornings and shut often enough for crashes and slips that we watch it before promising anyone a time. Once you are up on the Downs the driving is simple. The ground and the weather take over from there, and Warwick has two soils that behave nothing like each other.
locations.uses: hay, lucerne and chaff kept dry and away from mice on the Condamine flats, campdraft and rodeo gear stored properly between events instead of living in a float, saddlery, rugs and feed on the horse blocks through Yangan and Sladevale, fencing wire, posts and strainers on the grazing country running out toward Killarney, fruit bins, netting and irrigation fittings on the orchard blocks heading south into the granite belt, tools and stock overflow on the industrial land off the New England Highway, and a lockable store on a place where the shed filled up years ago
access: The run matters here more than it does closer to the coast. A Warwick delivery is a couple of hours west of Cornubia and the middle of the trip is Cunninghams Gap, a steep tight climb through the range that carries fog on most cold mornings, closes for crashes and slips more often than anybody would like, and eats time even on a good day. We schedule Warwick runs around that rather than pretending the trip is flat. Winter adds a second wrinkle that coastal customers never think about: heavy frost sits on the Downs until mid-morning through June and July, and a shaded frosted driveway is greasy in a way that has nothing to do with rain. Then there is the ground, and there are two Warwicks. North and west of town, out through Allora, Sladevale and the Condamine flats, it is black soil. Deep self-mulching cracking clay that opens into fissures wide enough to lose a boot in by October, then swells shut and turns to grease within an hour of a storm. Dry, it carries a loaded truck beautifully. Wet, it carries nothing at all, and it will not tell you which one it is doing until the wheels are already on it. Some of those paddocks are gilgai country too, so what looks like a flat approach is actually a series of shallow mounds and hollows. South and east toward Yangan, Killarney and the granite running down past Glen Aplin, the profile changes completely to decomposed granite, gravel and rock shelves under thin cover. Firm, but rarely level, and there is often a rock ledge sitting exactly where a corner casting wants to go. Town blocks are the straightforward part of the job. Warwick was laid out with wide streets and generous frontages, and most of the older sandstone-era addresses give a truck room to stand and swing that no coastal suburb would. What catches people out is the acreage: gates measured at the posts rather than at the narrowest point, grids nobody has ever rated, and a turning area at the far end that looked a lot bigger from the house verandah.

sections.h: Frost, forty-degree days and the water that appears inside
p: Warwick has one of the biggest daily temperature swings of anywhere we deliver. A July night in the minus figures followed by an afternoon in the high teens, or a February night at 18 after a day at 38, does something to a steel box that people are genuinely surprised by. Warm air holds moisture, the roof and walls cool faster than the air inside, and the moisture comes back out of the air onto the ceiling as condensation. It then drips onto whatever is underneath. Customers ring us about a leak, we go and look, and the roof is perfectly sound. It is the climate, not the container.

The fix is airflow and separation, and it costs almost nothing. Ask for vents at both ends when you order so air can cross the space rather than sit in it. Keep stock off the floor on pallets or bearers so air moves underneath. Do not seal the thing up tight in April and open it again in September expecting everything to be as you left it, particularly hay, leather, paper records or anything with a fabric surface. Where the contents genuinely cannot take moisture, a few desiccant hangers through a wet summer make a visible difference. And leave the doors open on a dry, breezy day now and then. Warwick gives you plenty of those.

sections.h: Horse country, and gear that only comes out four times a year
p: Warwick runs on horses and cattle, and a large slice of what we put on the ground here is storage for gear that is idle most of the year and then absolutely has to be ready. Campdraft and rodeo equipment, panels and portable yards, saddlery, rugs, tack and feed, the gear that goes on the float for a weekend at a show and then has to live somewhere for eleven weeks until the next one. A container beats a tarp and it beats the corner of a machinery shed, because it locks, it keeps birds and mice out, and it does not have a tractor reversed into it in March.

Delivery onto a horse property is as much about the animals as the ground. A tilt-tray unloading is a noisy piece of theatre, with hydraulics, chains and a steel box sliding down a steel bed. If horses are in a paddock the truck has to pass or in yards nearby, shift them before we arrive rather than after the truck is committed to a lane it cannot back out of. Tell us at the booking if gates need to stay shut behind us, if the arena is off limits, or if there is a preferred approach that keeps the truck away from the working end of the place.

sections.h: What goes underneath on cracking clay
p: Black soil moves further through the year than almost any ground in the country, and it does not move evenly across a paddock. It shrinks away through the dry and lifts back through the wet, and a container placed straight onto it will follow that movement one corner at a time. The frame is designed to carry everything through the four corner castings, so the moment those four points stop sitting at the same height the box starts working against itself and the doors stop lining up. Doors are the only part of a container you actually use, so a racked unit goes from useful to annoying fast.

On this country we would rather over-do the footings than come back. Wide concrete pads or a pair of long hardwood bearers spread the point load over a bigger patch than a single sleeper does, which matters when the soil underneath changes volume with the season. Put the door end on the high side of any fall so the doors swing with gravity. Keep the underside clear so air moves and water gets away instead of ponding against the bottom rail. Tell us at the quote what the ground is and roughly when it last rained, and we will bring the timber on the truck rather than leaving you a job for the weekend.

faqs.q: Does Cunninghams Gap actually affect when my container turns up in Warwick?
faqs.a: It does, and we would rather say so than invent a date. The Gap is the pinch point on the whole run from Cornubia. It fogs in on cold mornings, it closes for crashes and for landslips after heavy rain, and even when it is clear it is a slow climb for a loaded truck. Most Warwick deliveries land inside three to five business days. If you have a fixed date, a settlement, a show weekend or a contractor booked, tell us at the enquiry and we will build the run around it instead of explaining afterwards why it slipped.

faqs.q: Will a truck get across black soil paddocks after rain?
faqs.a: Not reliably, and we will not pretend otherwise. Black soil out through Allora and the Condamine flats is superb going when it is dry and completely impassable within an hour of a decent storm, and the surface gives away nothing about which state it is in. If your approach crosses it we will ring and shift the date rather than bog a truck and cut a trench across your paddock. Where there is a firm alternative such as a gravelled lane, a hardstand near the road or a spot by the shed that stays solid, tell us and we will use it.

faqs.q: Why does the inside of my container get wet in Warwick when the roof is fine?
faqs.a: Almost always condensation rather than a leak, and Warwick's temperature swing makes it more pronounced here than on the coast. Warm moist air inside meets a roof that has cooled off overnight and the moisture comes out onto the steel. Vents at both ends, contents kept up off the floor on pallets, and the doors opened on a dry day occasionally will handle most of it. If you are storing hay, leather, paper or anything else that will not forgive damp, mention it when you order and we will set the unit up with that in mind.

faqs.q: Can you deliver out into the granite country south of Warwick?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is a different job to a delivery on the flats. Down through Yangan, Killarney and the granite belt the ground is gravel, decomposed granite and rock shelf. It is firm, which helps, but it is almost never level and there is frequently rock right where a corner needs to sit. We build the low side up with sleepers or pads rather than cutting into the high side, because cutting in just makes a channel for water to run along beside the container. Send a photo of the spot and the approach and we will bring the right gear.

locations.name: Tweed Heads
locations.depot: our Cornubia yard, a straight run south down the motorway
locations.leadTime: Usually 2–4 business days; add a day where a crane or a body corporate window is involved
locations.truck: Tilt-tray where there is real side access; crane truck for canal blocks, villages and anything going over a fence
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Tweed Heads, Banora Point and Kingscliff. Cross-border rules, canal blocks and cane flats handled properly.
locations.line: Tweed Heads is one town with a state line drawn through the middle of it, and the line changes more than the postcode. Your neighbour two streets north is under a Queensland council and you are not, so the rules that apply to a container in their yard are not the rules that apply in yours. That trips people up constantly. The delivery itself is easy in the sense that the motorway drops a truck at your suburb in under an hour from Cornubia, and hard in the sense that the good streets down here were laid out around water rather than around trucks.
locations.uses: boat, jet ski, dive and fishing gear that never had a hope of fitting in the garage, storage for the trades working the constant rebuild from Banora Point to Kingscliff, cane and machinery gear on the river flats out toward Tumbulgum and Condong, stock and equipment for the tourism and short-stay operators along the beach strip, a lock-up for over-fifties village residents who downsized faster than they downsized their belongings, market and event gear that only comes out on weekends, and household storage while a Chinderah or Fingal cottage is knocked down and started again
access: The best and worst of a Tweed delivery are within a few kilometres of each other. The motorway and the Tweed Valley Way mean a truck reaches almost any address here quickly, but the last hundred metres varies enormously. The canal and waterfront lots at Tweed Heads West, Banora Point and around the Terranora Broadwater have the classic problem: wide at the water, narrow at the street, house across the full width of the block and a side gate you could not push a wheelbarrow through. Those are crane jobs, not tilt jobs, and the questions that decide them are all about what is overhead and how much room the outriggers get on a cul-de-sac that was drawn for cars. Older Tweed Heads South and Chinderah streets are tight in a different way, with short pitched driveways, low service lines and mature figs and poincianas hanging over the road at about four metres. Ground splits three ways across the shire. The beach side at Fingal Head, Kingscliff and Casuarina is dune sand over a high water table. It drains superbly and carries almost nothing, and a loaded truck will find the bottom of a nature strip that looked perfectly solid. The river flats out through Chinderah, Tumbulgum, Condong and Stotts Creek are old cane country, low and soft, and much of that lowland is acid sulfate soil, which is a genuine reason not to go digging footings for a container without asking someone first. Up on the Terranora and Bilambil ridges you get red basalt clay, firm and often steep, with driveways that pitch away hard at the kerb so a tilt bed grounds out before the container is clear. Add the retirement villages and gated communities, where a delivery needs body corporate approval, a booked window and sometimes a route that avoids a height-limited entry, and the pattern is clear. Almost everything here is deliverable. Very little of it is deliverable without a conversation first.

sections.h: One town, two sets of rules
p: The border runs through the middle of Tweed Heads and it matters. On the Queensland side, a container on a residential block is dealt with by one council under one planning scheme. On the New South Wales side, a few hundred metres away, it is a different council, a different scheme and different language about what counts as a temporary structure. People routinely look over the fence, see a container sitting happily in a Coolangatta yard and assume the same applies at their place in Tweed Heads South. It might. It might not.

We are not going to guess at the rule for your street, because it changes and it is yours to check before you order. What we can tell you is which questions get asked wherever you sit: how long is it staying, can it be seen from the road, is it storage or are you cutting doors and windows into it, and does an estate covenant or a body corporate have a say. Behind the building line, screened by a fence or a bit of planting, sitting level and out of a drainage path keeps almost everybody comfortable. Parked on the front lawn where the whole street can see it does not. Sort that before delivery, because moving a container twenty metres after the truck has gone is a second delivery, not an adjustment.

sections.h: Villages, gated estates and the booking that is not a booking
p: The Tweed has an unusually high share of over-fifties villages, resorts and gated communities, and they all work the same way: approval and a delivery window are two separate things and you need both. The body corporate or park manager will typically want written notice, a nominated time, evidence of insurance from the transport operator and a route that does not run under a height-limited entry or across a driveway they know will not carry weight. None of that is difficult. All of it is close to impossible to organise on the morning the truck is out the front.

Get the approval in hand first, then ring us with the window you have been given and we will build the run to land inside it. It is also worth checking what size the manager will actually accept, because plenty of villages will approve a 10ft or 20ft in a designated area and will not entertain a 40ft anywhere. If the container has to sit somewhere visible from a common area, ask about screening at the same time, since that is usually the condition that gets attached anyway.

sections.h: Sand at one end, cane flats at the other
p: There is no single answer to what goes under a container on the Tweed, because the ground changes character in the space of a few streets. On the beach side, dune sand is the issue. It looks firm, it carries poorly, and every corner casting is concentrating a couple of tonne onto a footprint the size of a dinner plate. Straight down onto sand or thin turf and it will settle unevenly inside a season, which is when the doors start needing a shoulder. On the old cane flats behind the river the problem is the opposite: low ground that holds water and stays soft well below a surface that looks dry.

Both want the same answer. Concrete pads or hardwood sleepers under the four corners, bedded and checked level both ways and on both diagonals, so the load spreads and the floor sits clear of the ground. Get it a hundred millimetres or more up and air moves underneath instead of damp sitting against the bearers for a decade, which matters far more here than it does inland. The other thing worth knowing on the lowlands is that a lot of that country is acid sulfate soil, so if your plan involves excavating for footings rather than sitting the unit on pads, that is a question for the council before it is a question for us.

faqs.q: Do Queensland or New South Wales rules apply to a container at Tweed Heads?
faqs.a: Whichever side of the border your title sits on, and in Tweed Heads that genuinely changes street by street. A block at Coolangatta or Bilinga is under a Queensland council and one planning scheme. Tweed Heads, Tweed Heads South, Banora Point and Kingscliff are New South Wales and a different scheme entirely. Do not assume the container you can see in a yard over the border tells you anything about your place. Check with your own council before you order, particularly if it is staying permanently, will be visible from the street, or is being cut about for a conversion.

faqs.q: Can you crane a container into a canal block at Banora Point or Tweed Heads West?
faqs.a: Yes, and on most waterfront lots it is the only way, because the house occupies the full width of the block and there is no usable side access. A crane truck stands on the street, lifts the container over the roofline and sets it in the back yard. What decides feasibility is reach and clearance: the horizontal distance from where the truck can legally stand, the height it has to clear, whether there are power or comms lines across your frontage, and whether the cul-de-sac gives room for the outriggers. Three photos, from the gate, from the back yard and looking up at the lines, usually settle it.

faqs.q: How fast can you get a container to the Tweed?
faqs.a: Two to four business days is the normal window, because the run south from Cornubia is short and the motorway does the work. What stretches it is a crane booking, a village or body corporate window we have to land inside, or wet weather on soft ground where waiting two days beats bogging a truck on your nature strip. If you have a hard date, tell us at the enquiry rather than after the booking is made and we will schedule around it.

faqs.q: Is there anything special about putting a container on the old cane flats?
faqs.a: Two things. The ground out through Chinderah, Tumbulgum and Condong is low and holds water, so it stays soft well under a surface that looks dry, and a container needs proper pads under the corners rather than being dropped onto turf. The second is that a lot of that lowland is acid sulfate soil, which becomes a real issue if you start excavating. Sitting a container on pads or sleepers avoids that problem entirely, which is one more reason we do it that way. Mention the ground when you enquire and we will bring the right materials.

locations.name: Ballina
locations.depot: our Cornubia yard or the Grafton depot, whichever is holding the grade and size you want
locations.leadTime: Usually 2–4 business days from order to on the ground
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; crane truck for 40ft, beach-suburb blocks and over-fence lifts
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Ballina, Lennox Head and Alstonville. Sand, high water table and tight beach streets planned for in advance.
locations.line: Ballina is two landscapes stacked on top of each other and the difference shows up the moment a truck arrives. Down at sea level you have the river mouth, the sand and a water table that is closer to the surface than anybody expects, and streets in the older beach pockets that were pegged out when a family car was a small thing. Fifteen minutes up the hill at Alstonville and Wollongbar it is deep red basalt, macadamia rows and a completely different set of problems. We ask which one you are on before we ask anything else.
locations.uses: trawler nets, pots, marine gear and outboard spares along the Richmond River fishing side of town, boards, skis and beach gear for households at Lennox Head and East Ballina where the garage capitulated years ago, macadamia husks, harvest gear and orchard equipment up on the Alstonville plateau, cane and machinery storage on the flats out toward Wardell and Broadwater, site stores for the trades working the Cumbalum and Skennars Head estates, dry storage for the small food and beverage makers scattered through the industrial estate, and household storage while a Ballina cottage is lifted and worked on
access: Getting to Ballina is the easy part now that the highway runs the way it does. Getting a truck into position is where the local knowledge earns its keep. The beach suburbs are the first constraint. Old East Ballina, the streets behind Shaws Bay, and the tighter parts of Lennox Head were subdivided small and close, with narrow carriageways, on-street parking on both sides, houses set hard against a boundary and side gates that are decorative rather than functional. On many of those a tilt-tray simply cannot be threaded down the side and the sensible answer is a crane lift from the road over the fence. Overhead services across the frontage and mature Norfolk pines and figs are part of that calculation. Then there is what is underneath. From the river mouth through East Ballina, Lennox and Skennars Head the profile is dune sand over a high water table, and around North Creek and the low ground behind the beaches the table is high enough that a post hole finds water. Sand drains beautifully and carries badly. A loaded truck can sit down to the axles on a nature strip that looked entirely solid, and a container corner casting will punch into it within a season if there is nothing spreading the load. Salt is the constant here too. Ballina sits in the wind off the Pacific and anything steel that has grass grown up around its base or leaf litter sitting on its roof will show it sooner than the same unit twenty kilometres inland. Up the hill it changes completely. The climb to Alstonville and Wollongbar puts you on deep red krasnozem basalt, which is superb soil and greasy going the moment it is wet, especially on the sloping orchard tracks between macadamia rows. Long private driveways up there tend to be crowned gravel with table drains, and they need real turning space at the top rather than optimistic turning space. The plateau roads also carry low canopy in stretches. A 20ft goes up without drama, a 40ft is a conversation about the approach before it is a conversation about price.

sections.h: Sand, water table and what actually holds it up
p: The single most common mistake on this coast is treating firm-looking sand as a foundation. It is not. Each corner casting on a loaded container concentrates a serious point load into a footprint the size of a dinner plate, and dune sand simply moves out of the way. What you get is uneven settlement, a frame that goes out of square and doors that need a shoulder inside the first year. The fix is cheap, permanent and takes minutes on delivery: concrete pads or hardwood sleepers under the four corners, bedded and checked level both ways and on both diagonals.

The high water table makes the second half of that matter more than it would elsewhere. A container floor sitting hard against damp sand never gets a chance to dry out underneath, and on a long-term store that is where problems start, from below rather than from the roof. Get it a hundred to a hundred and fifty millimetres clear so air moves under the bearers. It also makes life far easier if you ever want the thing lifted out again, because a container that has bedded itself into wet ground has to be dug free before a truck can get a chain on it. Tell us at the quote whether you are on sand, fill or a slab, and we will bring the materials and do the levelling as part of the delivery.

sections.h: Up the hill, into the macadamias
p: Alstonville, Wollongbar, Tintenbar and the country either side of the plateau road are a different job entirely. The soil is deep red basalt, which is why the macadamias are there, and it is beautiful ground until it rains. Then the orchard tracks and crowned gravel driveways get slick, the camber starts working against a loaded truck, and a wheel off the crown puts you in a table drain with nothing to do but wait for a tractor. We would rather ring and move a plateau delivery by two days than write off your driveway and half our afternoon.

The other plateau constraint is the shape of the block rather than the surface. Long driveways between tree rows are narrow by design and a tilt-tray needs to line up straight before it can unload, so turning space at the far end has to be genuine. Low canopy over the track catches people out too, because the bed on a tilt-tray goes up before the container comes off and it needs clear air above it. Send a photo from the gate looking down the drive and one of the spot itself with its surroundings, and we will tell you what will make it up there before anybody books a truck.

sections.h: Salt air, and the maintenance that is not really maintenance
p: A shipping container spent its working life at sea, so salt is not new to it. What is new is standing still. On a ship it is moving through clean air and getting rained on and dried off constantly. In a Lennox Head back yard it sits under a tree with leaf litter building up on the roof and kikuyu growing up over the bottom rail, and that is what actually starts surface corrosion, far more than the breeze off the water does. Wet leaves held against a roof panel for six months, and long grass trapping moisture against the steel, are the two things worth eliminating.

The whole regime is a sweep of the roof a couple of times a year, a whipper snipper around the base, keeping the underside clear of stacked timber and drums so water and air can get away, and leaving the doors open on a dry breezy day now and then so any condensation clears. That is it. On this coast it is the difference between a unit that looks tired in five years and one that is still square and solid in twenty. If it is going to live outdoors permanently within sight of the water, ask us about grade when you order rather than after, and we will point you at the right one for the job instead of the dearest one on the list.

faqs.q: Will a container sink into the sand at Lennox Head or East Ballina?
faqs.a: It will settle unevenly if it goes straight onto sand or thin turf, and the first symptom is doors that stop closing cleanly. Sand drains brilliantly and carries very little, and each corner casting is a large point load in a small footprint. Concrete pads or hardwood sleepers under the four corners, bedded level, fix it permanently. On the beach side it is worth going a step further and getting the floor properly clear of the ground, because the water table here is high and a floor sitting against damp sand never dries out. Mention the ground when you enquire and we will bring what is needed on the truck.

faqs.q: There is no side access at my place. Can you still deliver?
faqs.a: Usually, with a crane truck lifting from the street over the fence into the yard. That is routine in the older beach streets around East Ballina and Lennox where the house sits hard against a boundary. What decides it is reach and clearance: how far the container has to travel horizontally, what height it has to clear, whether there are service lines across your frontage, and whether the street is wide enough for the outriggers with cars parked. Take a photo from the front gate, one from the back yard looking toward the street, and one straight up at the lines, and we can usually answer the same day.

faqs.q: Can you get a container up to an Alstonville or Wollongbar orchard block?
faqs.a: Regularly, and the plateau is good delivering country in the dry. What stops us is red basalt after rain, which turns greasy fast on a crowned gravel driveway or a track between macadamia rows, plus low canopy over the drive and turning space at the top that is not as big as it looked. A 20ft goes up comfortably. A 40ft needs the approach checked first, and where it will not work, two 20ft placed end to end usually gives more useful space anyway. Send photos of the gate, the drive and the spot.

faqs.q: Where does a Ballina container actually come from?
faqs.a: Either our Cornubia yard north of the border or the depot at Grafton, depending on which one is holding the size and grade you want that week. Practically that means two chances at getting you the exact unit rather than one, and it usually means two to four business days from order to on the ground. If you want to look at a container before it arrives, ask and we will send photos of the actual unit on request before delivery, including the corners, the door end, the roof and the internal floor.

locations.name: Lismore
locations.depot: the Grafton depot, run north up the highway and across on the Bruxner
locations.leadTime: Usually 2–4 business days from order to on the ground
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; crane truck for 40ft, the older narrow streets and anything lifted over a fence
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Lismore and Goonellabah. Honest advice on height above water, steep basalt driveways and old narrow streets.
locations.line: Nobody in Lismore needs a container company to explain water to them. This town has a better collective memory of levels and heights than any document we could write, and the people asking us questions here are usually asking a sharper version of them than we get anywhere else. So we will be blunt about what a container is and is not, and then talk about the things that actually make a difference: where it sits, how high it sits, and what happens on the streets and the driveways between the flats and the hill.
locations.uses: site storage for the trades still working through repairs and rebuilds across the basin, tools and materials for owner-builders doing the work themselves, household contents kept somewhere secure while a place is stripped back and started again, macadamia and small-crop gear on the farms out through Dunoon, Clunes and Modanville, beef and fencing equipment on the grazing country toward Casino, stock and equipment for businesses working out of premises that are smaller than they used to be, and gear storage for the sporting clubs, halls and community groups that lost sheds
access: Lismore is a basin with a river through it and a ridge on one side, and the delivery changes completely depending on which part you are in. Down on the flats through South Lismore, North Lismore, the CBD fringe and the streets behind Union Street, the housing stock is old, timber and mostly up on stumps. The subdivisions are tight, the carriageways are narrow with cars on both sides, driveways are short and pitch away hard at the kerb so a tilt bed grounds out before a container is clear, and the side gates were set out for a wheelbarrow. On top of that there are enormous camphor laurels through those streets, dropping limbs at exactly the height a raised tilt bed wants to occupy. A good share of those addresses are crane jobs rather than tilt jobs and it is far better to know that at the quote than at seven in the morning. The ground on the flats is river alluvium, deep silt that has been laid down and re-laid for a very long time. It is superb soil and it is a liar underfoot. It dries hard, it looks like hardstand, then a wet week goes through it and a corner casting carrying a couple of tonne sinks a hundred millimetres while you watch. Up on the hill it is a different world. Goonellabah, East Lismore and Girards Hill sit on red basalt, and the driveways up there are steep, often with a crest or a sharp break of grade at the kerb that will ground a truck bed just as reliably as a soft flat will bog one. Basalt is firm going when dry and slippery within minutes of rain. Then there is the rural country out toward Dunoon, Clunes, Modanville and Nimbin, which brings crowned gravel driveways, table drains, causeways that come up quickly after rain in the hills above you, and gates that measure less than they look. Whatever the address, three photos settle most of it: one from the middle of the road looking in, one down the length of the approach, and one of the spot itself.

sections.h: Height is the only thing that helps
p: We are going to be direct, because in Lismore the polite version is useless. A shipping container is not flood protection and we will not sell it as such. A cargo-worthy unit is checked wind and watertight, and what that means is rain from above, on a roof, on a container standing upright. It says nothing about water rising against the doors. Floodwater that reaches the door sill gets past the seals and comes in, because door seals are built to shed rain running down a face, not to hold back a head of water pushing against them. Anyone who tells you otherwise is selling you something they should not be.

The second thing is buoyancy, and this town saw it. An empty or lightly loaded container is a very large sealed steel box, and in deep water it will float, turn and travel. Containers moved in 2022. That is not a theoretical risk here. So the useful conversation is not about the box, it is about where you put it and how high. Site it on the highest usable ground on the property rather than the flattest. Keep it out of the overland flow path, because plenty of damage in the basin comes from water running across blocks rather than from the river alone. And if the contents are genuinely irreplaceable, height beats every other decision you will make about it.

sections.h: Getting it up off the ground, properly
p: The practical follow-on from that is elevation, and there is a right and a wrong way to do it. Setting a container up on stacked blocks, a raised pad or a purpose-built stand does two useful things at once: it lifts the floor above ordinary nuisance water and it keeps the underside dry and ventilated so the bearers are not sitting in damp silt for a decade. It also makes the unit easier to lift and shift later, which matters more than people think on a block that might be reconfigured.

How high and how it is engineered is a question for someone qualified when you are going beyond routine levelling, because a container up on stands is carrying its whole load through four points and those points now have to be built to take it. We will do the ordinary work as part of delivery, which means concrete pads or hardwood sleepers under the corner castings, checked level both ways and on both diagonals, with the door end on the high side of any fall so the doors swing with gravity. Beyond that, if the plan is a serious elevated stand on the flats, get it designed rather than improvised. On the alluvium down there, spreading the load matters as much as the height does.

sections.h: Rebuild work, and why hire suits it
p: A lot of what we put on the ground around Lismore is tied to work with an end date on it. A house being stripped and reworked, a shop fitted out again, a shed rebuilt, an owner-builder doing it themselves across eighteen months of weekends. For all of that, hire earns its keep. You are not tying up capital in something you will be trying to move on the moment the job finishes, you are not the one arranging a truck at the far end, and if the job changes shape you can swap the container for a bigger or smaller one instead of selling and buying again.

Buying gets better the moment the timeframe goes vague or the container becomes part of how the place works permanently, and there is a real second-hand market in the Northern Rivers if you ever want out. What decides it is usually simpler than people expect: how long, what is going inside, and whether it needs to be dry. Tell us those three and we will point you at the right size and grade instead of the dearest one. The full explanation of what each grade is and what it is checked for sits on our grades page, which is a better place to read it than a locality page.

faqs.q: Is a shipping container safe from floodwater in Lismore?
faqs.a: No, and we will not dress that up. A container is checked for weather from above, not for water rising against the doors. Floodwater that reaches the door sill gets past the seals and gets inside, and an empty container is a sealed steel box that will float, turn and move once the water is deep enough. That happened here in 2022. What protects contents is height and siting: the highest usable ground on the block, out of the overland flow path, and set up on a raised pad or stand if it is a long-term store on the flats.

faqs.q: Can you put a container up on stands or blocks so the floor sits higher?
faqs.a: We can set a unit on concrete pads or hardwood sleepers as part of the delivery, level in both directions with the door end on the high side, and that lifts the floor clear of the ground and keeps the underside ventilated. If you want a genuinely elevated stand, well above routine levelling, get it designed by someone qualified. A container carries everything through its four corner castings, so once it is up in the air those four points have to be built to take the load. Tell us the plan at the quote and we will place it to suit.

faqs.q: Can a truck get into the narrow streets in South and North Lismore?
faqs.a: Often, but not always with a tilt-tray. Those streets are narrow with cars parked both sides, the driveways are short and break away hard at the kerb so the bed grounds out before the container is clear, and there are big camphor laurels dropping limbs right where a raised bed needs air. On plenty of those addresses a crane truck lifting from the road over the fence is quicker and safer than trying to thread a tilt down the side. Send a photo from the middle of the road looking at the house and we will call it.

faqs.q: How long does delivery take to Lismore, and where does the container come from?
faqs.a: Stock for the Northern Rivers is held at our Grafton depot, which is a straightforward run north, so two to four business days from order to on the ground is the normal window. What stretches it is a crane booking or wet weather on soft ground, where waiting a couple of days beats bogging a truck on your block. If you want to see the unit first, inspection at Grafton can be arranged, or ask for photos of the actual container on request and we will send them before delivery.

locations.name: Grafton
locations.depot: stock held locally at our Grafton depot, with inspection by arrangement
locations.leadTime: Often next business day, and usually inside two
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; crane truck or side loader for 40ft and for the older streets either side of the river
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Grafton, with stock held locally. Fast delivery across the Clarence Valley and straight advice on river ground.
locations.line: Grafton is one of the handful of towns where we hold stock on the ground rather than sending it up a highway, and that changes the whole shape of the transaction. You are not waiting on a truck from a capital city, you are not paying for a long cartage buried in a price, and if something needs to be swapped it is a short run rather than a lost day. Inspection is by arrangement, so ring first and we will organise a time to walk you round the units rather than have you turn up to a gate.
locations.uses: cane and machinery gear on the flats running down the Clarence toward Ulmarra and Harwood, beef, fencing and fodder storage on the grazing country out through Coutts Crossing and Copmanhurst, timber, tools and mill equipment around the industrial area at Koolkhan and South Grafton, nets, pots and marine gear for the fishing side of the valley at Maclean, Yamba and Iluka, netting, bins and irrigation fittings on the blueberry and small-crop blocks spreading north, site stores for builders working the estates at Junction Hill and Clarenza, and dry storage on the river blocks where a shed is not an option
access: Having stock in town changes what is possible with a booking, and it changes what happens when something goes wrong. Next business day is genuinely on the table for a standard 20ft going to an address with clear access, we can be flexible when weather pushes a date, and a container that turns out to be the wrong size for the spot is a short run back rather than a full day of cartage. After that, Grafton is a river town and it behaves like one. The valley floor either side of the Clarence is deep alluvial silt and sand ridges, and the two do not behave the same way. The silt flats are excellent soil that dries into something that looks and feels like hardstand, then goes soft a long way down after a wet week, so a corner casting will sink while you are standing there watching it. The sand ridges through parts of South Grafton and Junction Hill drain fast and carry poorly, which is a different route to the same result. Both want the container on pads rather than straight onto turf. The town itself divides at the river. Central Grafton is a grid of wide streets with generous frontages, which is good delivering country, but it is also the jacaranda town and there is a very large amount of mature canopy sitting at four metres over the road and over the driveways. A tilt-tray raises its bed before the container comes off and it needs clear air above it, so a street that a truck drives down comfortably is not automatically a street it can unload in. South Grafton and the older river-side pockets are tighter, with short pitched driveways and low service lines. Out of town the valley opens up and the constraints become rural: long crowned gravel driveways with table drains, causeways on the tributaries that come up fast after rain in the ranges to the west even when it is dry over you, cattle grids nobody has ever rated, and gates that measure narrower at the swing than they do at the posts.

sections.h: Local stock, and what that is actually worth to you
p: Most container sellers quoting a Clarence Valley job are working from a depot several hours away, which means the truck runs the highway both directions and that trip is in your number whether it is itemised or not. We hold stock at a depot here in Grafton. Practically, that shows up in three ways. It shows up in speed, because next business day is a real option rather than a marketing line. It shows up in flexibility, because if rain has turned your approach to grease we can move the date by two days without it costing anybody a full day of cartage. And it shows up when something is not right, because a swap is a short run rather than a negotiation.

It also means you can look at the actual unit rather than a photograph of something similar. Inspection here is by arrangement rather than a walk-in yard, so ring on 1300 467 776 and we will set a time when someone can meet you and the container you are interested in is accessible. If the drive does not suit, ask for photos of the actual unit on request and we will send them before delivery, including the corner posts, the door end, the roof and the internal floor. Not a stock photo of something similar, the one that is coming to you.

sections.h: A river town, and where the container should sit
p: Grafton knows the Clarence well and there is a levee here for a reason, so let us be straight about what a container does and does not do. It is checked for weather from above. That is rain on a roof. It is not a barrier against water rising against the doors, because door seals are designed to shed rain running down a face, not to hold back a head of water pushing on them. Water that reaches the sill gets past the seals and gets inside. And an empty container is a large sealed steel box that will float and travel once the water is deep enough, which is worth thinking about on a block that has seen it before.

So the decision that matters is siting. Put it on the highest usable part of the block rather than the most convenient one, keep it clear of the overland flow path across the property, and if it is a long-term store on low ground talk to us about setting it up on pads or a raised base so the floor sits higher and the underside stays dry and ventilated. On the silt down here, spreading the load over a decent footprint matters as much as the height does, because that soil will let a concentrated point load down further than you would expect.

sections.h: What the valley actually uses them for
p: The Clarence is a working valley and the containers we put out here work. Cane and machinery gear on the river flats. Beef, fencing and fodder on the grazing country west and south. Timber and mill equipment through Koolkhan and South Grafton. Nets, pots, ropes and outboard spares down at the mouth around Maclean, Yamba and Iluka, where salt air makes a lockable steel box the sensible answer for gear that would otherwise live under a tarp. And an increasing amount of horticulture, with blueberry and small-crop blocks needing netting, bins, fittings and chemicals stored securely and out of the weather.

That mix is the reason we hold a spread of sizes here rather than a single popular one. A 10ft suits a small holding, a workshop corner or a club that needs gear locked up and nothing more. A 20ft is the workhorse and handles most farm and trade requirements. A 40ft gives machinery-length storage where the approach is good, and out on the flats the approach usually is. Where a driveway is tight but the volume is genuinely needed, two 20ft with a gap between them and a roof across the middle is a very common setup in this valley and it gives you a covered working bay for nothing much.

faqs.q: Can I look at a container in Grafton before I buy it?
faqs.a: Yes, by arrangement. We hold stock at a depot in Grafton, but it is not a walk-in retail yard, so ring on 1300 467 776 first and we will set a time when someone can meet you and the unit you are interested in is accessible. You can open the doors, look down the floor and check the seals yourself rather than taking anybody's word for the condition. If the trip does not suit, ask for photos of the actual container on request and we will send them before delivery, including the corners, the door end and the internal floor.

faqs.q: How quickly can you deliver a container in the Clarence Valley?
faqs.a: Faster than most, because the stock is already here rather than several hours up or down the highway. Next business day happens regularly on a standard 20ft going to an address with clear access, and inside two days is the normal expectation. What stretches it is a crane booking, a unit that needs a lockbox or vents fitted before it goes, or wet weather on soft ground where waiting beats bogging a truck on your place. Tell us your date at the enquiry and we will build the run around it.

faqs.q: Do the jacarandas actually get in the way of a delivery in Grafton?
faqs.a: More often than you would think, and it catches out people who assume a wide street means an easy job. A tilt-tray raises its bed a long way before the container slides off, so it needs clear air above, not just a lane to drive down. Mature canopy hanging at around four metres over a street or a driveway is a genuine constraint, and central Grafton has a lot of it. If your frontage is under a big tree, tell us or send a photo looking up, and we will bring a crane truck or find another position rather than discovering it on the day.

faqs.q: Is a container a good store on a Clarence River flat?
faqs.a: For weather, vermin and security, yes, and it is one of the most common things we do out here. For rising water, no. A container is checked for rain from above, not for water pushing against the doors, and floodwater that reaches the sill will get past the seals. An empty one will also float once the water gets deep enough. Site it on the highest usable ground, keep it out of the overland flow path, and set it on pads or a raised base so the floor sits clear and the underside can breathe.

locations.name: Mullumbimby
locations.depot: our Cornubia yard, run down the highway and in off the Brunswick Valley Way
locations.leadTime: Usually 3–5 business days; back-road addresses are scheduled around the weather
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft on most valley blocks; 40ft only where the approach has been checked, and often two 20ft instead
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Mullumbimby and the Byron hinterland. One-lane bridges, creek crossings and shared access tracks allowed for.
locations.line: The town is not the problem. Mullumbimby itself is a short grid you can deliver into on a Tuesday morning without much thought. It is what happens after you turn off the flat that decides everything, because within ten minutes of the main street you can be on a one-lane bridge, then a causeway, then four kilometres of red dirt climbing a spur with a rainforest canopy meeting overhead. We do those runs regularly. We just want to know which one we are on before a truck leaves the yard, not when it is halfway up.
locations.uses: macadamia and avocado harvest gear, bins and orchard equipment through the Brunswick Valley, tools, timber and materials for owner-builders working slowly on a hinterland block, storage for the market stallholders and small-batch food and beverage makers the shire is full of, feed, tack and fencing on the small holdings out through Wilsons Creek and Upper Main Arm, shared equipment and supplies on multiple-occupancy properties where nobody has a big enough shed, gear for the festivals and events that come and go, and a dry lock-up on a block where a shed would mean starting a planning conversation
access: Everything about a hinterland delivery here is decided by the road in. The valleys behind Mullumbimby, through Main Arm, Upper Main Arm, Wilsons Creek, Huonbrook, Goonengerry and Federal, are narrow, steep and stitched with watercourses. There are one-lane bridges with weight and width limits posted on them, and there are causeways rather than bridges on plenty of the crossings, which come up quickly after rain in the range above you even when it has not rained where you are standing. A causeway with water over it is not a maybe for a loaded truck, it is a no, and it can stay a no for a day or two after the sky clears. There are also stretches that have been repaired since the 2022 slips and are narrower or rougher than they were. The surface is the second factor. This is red basalt country and the sealed sections give way to formed gravel and then to red dirt fast. Red basalt is superb ground when dry and genuinely greasy within minutes of a shower, particularly on a climb with a camber to it, and a loaded rigid truck loses traction long before an unloaded one does. Overhead is the third. The canopy through these valleys is subtropical rainforest, camphor laurel and big old figs, and it hangs low over the road in long stretches. A tilt-tray needs its bed raised high before a container comes off, so clear air above matters as much as clear road ahead. Then the blocks themselves. Long shared driveways with a crown and table drains. Gates set at an angle to the track. Turning space at the far end that has to be real rather than hopeful, because reversing a rigid truck four kilometres back down a spur road in the dark is nobody's idea of an afternoon. And rock ledges and side-cut benches where the container has to sit, which is a levelling job rather than a drop. A 20ft handles almost all of this. A 40ft is a proper conversation and quite often the honest answer is two 20ft.

sections.h: One-lane bridges, causeways and the date that moves
p: We would rather ring you and shift a delivery by two days than send a loaded truck at a rising causeway or onto a red dirt climb that has gone to grease. Nobody wins from a bogged truck. Not you, watching it cut a trench across your access and wondering who is paying for the tractor, and not us, with a truck and a driver tied up for the rest of the day and a container sitting somewhere it was never meant to be. So we build a bit of slack into hinterland bookings, particularly through summer, and we ring and tell you what is happening rather than leaving you at home waiting for something that was never going to make it.

Your local knowledge is worth more than any map here. You know which of your crossings goes over first and how long it takes to drop. You know whether the gravel section on your road holds together or turns. You know that the bridge on the way in has a limit posted on it, and what that limit is. Tell us at the booking. If there is a firm alternative, a neighbour's sealed access, a hardstand near the bitumen, a spot by the shed that stays solid whatever the weather, that is often the difference between this week and next. And if the road has just been graded, say so, because a freshly graded surface has no bind in it and will not hold a loaded truck until traffic and a bit of weather have worked it.

sections.h: Shared access, shared decisions
p: A lot of land around Mullumbimby is held as multiple occupancy or community title, and that changes a delivery in ways a suburban address never does. The access track is shared, so it is somebody's job to maintain it and it may not be the person ordering the container. There can be a gate arrangement, a locked chain, an agreed speed on the track and a group that expects notice before a twenty-tonne truck comes through. There may also be an internal decision to make about where a container can sit, which is a slower process than ringing us.

None of that is a problem, it just needs to happen before the booking rather than after. Sort out who is opening the gate, whether the track is passable for a rigid truck in its current condition, whether anyone needs notice, and exactly where the container is going. Then ring us with the answers. The other thing worth raising early is size, because on a shared track the constraint is usually the tightest corner on the whole run rather than anything on your own patch, and that corner may be a kilometre from your building envelope.

sections.h: Levelling on a side-cut bench
p: Almost nothing in these valleys is level, and a container does not need it to be. What it needs is four corners at the same height. On a hillside block that means building the low side up with stacked hardwood sleepers or pads set into the fall, rather than cutting the high side away. Cutting in feels tidier and is a mistake, because it creates a shelf that water runs along and ponds against the bottom rail every time it rains, and on this country it rains properly.

Red basalt is firm to carry a load once it is dry, but it holds water and it will let a concentrated point load down if there is nothing spreading it, so the pads want to be wider than they look necessary. Put the door end on the high side of the fall so the doors swing with gravity rather than against it, keep the grass down and the underside clear so air and water can get away, and sweep the leaf litter off the roof if it is going in under canopy, because wet leaves held against a roof panel for six months is what actually starts corrosion. Get all that right on the day and the unit will still be square and opening cleanly in twenty years.

faqs.q: Can you deliver up Main Arm or Wilsons Creek?
faqs.a: Yes, and we do it regularly, but the road decides the size and the date. Those runs have one-lane bridges with posted limits, causeways that come up fast after rain in the range above, sections repaired since the 2022 slips that are narrower than they used to be, and low rainforest canopy over long stretches. A 20ft on a tilt-tray is the reliable option. Tell us at the enquiry which crossings are on your approach and how they behave after rain, and send a photo from the gate looking down the track.

faqs.q: Why does the wet weather move my delivery when it is not raining at my place?
faqs.a: Because the water that closes your causeway usually fell somewhere above you. Rain in the range behind Mullumbimby runs into the creeks and puts crossings under in the valleys below with a clear sky overhead. On top of that, red basalt gravel goes slick within minutes of a shower and stays that way on a shaded climb long after the surface looks dry. We build slack into hinterland bookings through summer for exactly that reason, and we ring rather than leaving you waiting on a truck that will not make it.

faqs.q: Can I get a 40ft container onto a hinterland block?
faqs.a: Sometimes, and the limiting factor is almost never the block. It is the tightest corner, the narrowest bridge and the lowest branch between the highway and your gate. A 40ft on a side loader is a very different vehicle to a 20ft on a tilt-tray and on a lot of these roads it simply will not get there safely. Where you genuinely need the length, two 20ft placed end to end usually delivers more useful and more flexible space with a far simpler delivery, and you can put a roof across the gap and gain a covered bay.

faqs.q: The access track is shared with other properties. What do you need from us?
faqs.a: Four things, and all of them before the booking rather than on the day. Who is opening the gate and will they be there. Whether the track in its current condition will carry a loaded rigid truck the whole way, including any bridges or causeways. Whether the other residents need notice. And exactly where the container is going, since on community-title land that is often a decision for the group rather than for one household. Sort those out, ring us with the answers, and the delivery itself is usually the easy part of the day.

locations.name: Coffs Harbour
locations.depot: the Grafton depot, an easy run south down the highway
locations.leadTime: Usually 2–4 business days from order to on the ground
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; crane truck for 40ft, steep hillside blocks and anything lifted over a fence
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Coffs Harbour, Sawtell and Woolgoolga. Steep escarpment driveways, banana and blueberry country, tight estates.
locations.line: There is nowhere else on this coast where the range comes down this hard to the sea, and it shapes every delivery in Coffs. The flat land is a thin strip between the surf and the hills, and the moment you leave it you are on a slope, which is why the bananas ended up planted on grades no tractor should be on. Half the addresses we go to have a driveway that pitches off the kerb steeply enough to ground a tilt bed, and the other half are on sand behind a beach. The good news is the stock is only an hour and a bit north at Grafton.
locations.uses: netting, bins, irrigation fittings and harvest gear on the blueberry and banana blocks running from Boambee up through Corindi and Woolgoolga, nets, pots and outboard spares for the boats working out of the harbour and the jetty, boards, skis and beach gear for households at Sawtell, Emerald Beach and Sapphire, site stores for the builders working the hill estates and the ongoing highway and bypass works, gear storage for the sporting clubs and events that fill this town, timber and tools on the escarpment blocks running up toward Bellingen and Dorrigo, and household storage during a knockdown or a move
access: Coffs is a slope with a town on it. The escarpment runs almost to the water, so once you are off the highway flat and into Korora, Diggers Beach, Boambee East, Toormina's higher streets, Coramba Road or the hill above the Jetty, you are dealing with driveways that fall away hard at the kerb and then climb, often with a sharp break of grade right at the property line. That break is what grounds a tilt bed before the container is clear, and it is not always visible from the seat of a car. Add hairpin bends on some of the older hillside subdivisions and turning space that runs out at the top, and a decent share of hillside addresses end up being crane jobs. On the beach side, at Sawtell, Sapphire, Emerald Beach and Moonee, it is dune sand over a high water table, which drains fast and carries almost nothing, so a loaded truck will find the bottom of a nature strip and a corner casting will punch straight through thin turf. Inland it changes to red basalt and clay on the plantation slopes, which is firm in the dry and greasy within minutes of rain, especially on the steep tracks between banana or blueberry rows and under the netting where the ground never really gets sun on it. The other current factor is the roadworks. The bypass build has changed traffic patterns through town, closed and rerouted access in places and put a lot of heavy vehicle movement onto roads that were already busy, which is why we give a delivery window rather than an hour. Then there are the newer estates, at Sandy Beach, Bonville, Moonee and the hill pockets, which bring narrow streets with cars parked both sides, service pits and stormwater grates on the kerb line that will crack under a loaded rear axle, fill that has not settled, and covenants that will have something to say about where a steel box may sit. West of town the Waterfall Way climb toward Bellingen and Dorrigo is a genuinely steep, tightly wound haul, and size gets decided by that road rather than by your block.

sections.h: Steep driveways, and when it becomes a crane job
p: The classic Coffs problem is a driveway that drops off the kerb, crosses a stormwater channel and then climbs to a house sitting well above the road. Every one of those elements works against a tilt-tray. The bed has to lift high before the container slides, the truck needs its chassis clear underneath, and a sharp break of grade at the property line will have the rear of the bed touching down while the container is still on it. A crest halfway up does the same thing from the other direction. None of that means we cannot deliver, it means the truck changes.

A crane truck stands on the street and places the container where it needs to go, over a fence, a carport or a bank. What decides feasibility is reach and clearance: the horizontal distance from where the truck can legally stand to the spot, the height of anything in between, whether there are power or comms lines across your frontage, and whether the street is wide enough for the outriggers, which on a narrow hillside road with cars parked can mean holding traffic for a while. One photo taken from the middle of the road looking straight up the drive, one from the spot looking back at the street, and one straight up at the lines will usually let us call it before anybody talks about price.

sections.h: Bananas, blueberries and gear that has to lock
p: Horticulture is the reason a lot of containers land in this district. The banana blocks are still there on the steep ground and the blueberry industry has spread across a great deal of country from Boambee north through Corindi and Woolgoolga, and both generate the same requirement: a large volume of gear that must be secure, dry and vermin-proof, on a block where a shed either does not exist or is already full. Netting and clips, harvest bins and crates, irrigation fittings, pumps, spray equipment, chemicals that have to be locked, picking gear that arrives with a crew and goes away again.

A container suits that because it arrives finished, it needs no slab poured and cured first, it is lockable on the day it lands, and it can be relocated or sold on if the planting changes. On sloping plantation ground it also beats a shed, because a container can be levelled on pads where a slab would mean serious excavation on a grade. The practical constraints are the tracks between rows, which are narrow and cambered and go slick fast, and the netting itself, which is often low enough to rule out a raised tilt bed. Tell us where in the block it is going and what the approach looks like and we will work out whether it is a tilt job, a crane job, or a drop on firm ground for you to shift in with the tractor.

sections.h: Estates, covenants and the retirement end of town
p: Coffs has a large and growing share of lifestyle estates and over-fifties communities, and they are consistently the strictest environments we deliver into. Estate covenants sit on top of the council position and are frequently tighter than it, with something to say about what may be stored on a lot, whether it can be visible from the street, what colours are acceptable and whether anything may sit forward of the building line. Village and community managers usually want written notice, a nominated window, insurance details from the transport operator and a route that avoids a height-limited entry.

We will not guess at the rule for your particular street, because it varies and it is yours to check before you order. The pattern is consistent enough to plan around though: temporary, behind the building line, screened by a fence or planting and used for storage is the easy end. Permanent, prominent and altered is where the questions start. It is also worth asking the manager or the estate what size they will accept, because plenty will approve a 10ft or 20ft in a nominated position and will not entertain a 40ft at all. Get that settled first and then ring us with the window, and we will land the truck inside it.

faqs.q: My driveway is steep. Can you still get a container in?
faqs.a: Usually, but often not with a tilt-tray. Where a Coffs driveway drops hard off the kerb and then climbs, or has a sharp break of grade at the property line, the truck bed touches down before the container is clear. A crest partway up does the same. On those blocks we look at a crane truck placing it over the fence or the bank instead, or at a smaller unit than the one originally planned. Send a photo taken from the middle of the road looking straight up the drive and another from where the container is going, and we can usually answer on the spot.

faqs.q: How long does delivery take to Coffs Harbour?
faqs.a: Two to four business days is the normal window, because stock is held at our Grafton depot rather than several hours away. What can stretch it is a crane booking, an estate or village window we have to land inside, wet weather on a plantation track or a sandy block, and the traffic effects of the bypass works, which are the reason we give a window rather than an hour. If you have a fixed date, tell us at the enquiry and we will build the run around it.

faqs.q: Can you deliver onto a blueberry or banana block?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is a good part of what we do here. The things to check first are the width and camber of the track between rows, how the surface behaves after rain, since red basalt and clay go greasy within minutes, and the height of any netting, because a tilt-tray raises its bed a long way before the container comes off. Where the row access will not take a truck, the usual answer is to set the container down on firm ground near the shed or the road for you to walk in with the tractor at your own pace.

faqs.q: Can I inspect a container before it is delivered to Coffs?
faqs.a: Yes. Stock for this coast is held at our Grafton depot, roughly an hour and a half north, and inspection there is by arrangement rather than a walk-in yard, so ring on 1300 467 776 and we will set a time when someone can meet you. If the trip is not worth it, ask for photos of the actual unit on request and we will send them before delivery, including the corner posts, the door end, the roof and the internal floor, so you are looking at the container that is coming to you rather than one like it.

locations.depot: the Grafton depot, on a scheduled run south down the highway
locations.leadTime: Usually 4–7 business days, scheduled around the southbound run
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; crane truck for 40ft, village deliveries and anything lifted over a fence
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Port Macquarie, Wauchope and Lake Cathie. Coastal sand, backswamp ground and estate covenants dealt with plainly.
locations.line: Port Macquarie is the furthest south we run from the Grafton depot, and we will be straight about what that means: this is a scheduled run rather than a next-day town, so the honest window is four to seven business days and we would rather quote that than promise Tuesday and ring you on Thursday. What you get in exchange is a truck that arrives knowing what it is walking into, which on the Hastings matters, because between the dune sand, the backswamp behind it and the covenants in the newer estates there is plenty to walk into.
locations.uses: oyster gear, punts, baskets and marine equipment on the Hastings and down through the Camden Haven, boards, boats and beach gear for households at Lake Cathie, Bonny Hills and Port itself, timber, tools and mill equipment around Wauchope, beef and dairy gear on the river flats out through Beechwood and Rollands Plains, site stores for the trades working the Thrumster and Sovereign Hills builds, downsizers who moved into a village and found the storage cage was optimistic, storage for the events, markets and sporting clubs the town runs on, and dry storage on the escarpment blocks toward Comboyne
access: Ground is the first conversation on the Hastings and it changes over very short distances. The coastal strip from Port itself down through Lake Cathie, Bonny Hills and North Haven is dune sand over a shallow water table. It drains superbly and carries almost nothing, so a loaded truck sits down into a nature strip that looked perfectly firm, and a corner casting punches through thin turf inside a season. Behind the dunes there is backswamp, low ground that holds water and stays soft a long way below a surface that looks dry, and much of that lowland is acid sulfate country, which matters the moment anybody starts talking about digging footings rather than sitting a unit on pads. Inland along the Hastings and Wilson river flats through Wauchope, Beechwood and Rollands Plains it is alluvium, excellent ground that goes to grease after rain and comes up quickly when the river runs. The town itself splits into old and new. The older streets around the CBD, Settlement City and the coastal pockets have short pitched driveways, houses close to the boundary, mature figs and Norfolk pines and low service lines across the frontage, so a crane lift over the fence is frequently the sensible answer. The newer estates at Thrumster, Sovereign Hills, Sancrox and the growth areas out toward the highway have the standard pattern of narrow streets, cars parked both sides, service pits and stormwater grates on the kerb line that will crack under a loaded rear axle, cut-and-fill blocks where the ground has not finished settling, and covenants that will have an opinion about a steel box. Then there is the escarpment. The climbs west toward Comboyne and up through Byabarra are steep, tightly wound and narrow, with low canopy in stretches and turning space that runs out at the top of long private driveways. Those runs are 20ft country. A 40ft up there is a conversation about the approach long before it is a conversation about the container.

sections.h: A scheduled run, and why we tell you that up front
p: Stock for this stretch of coast comes from our Grafton depot, which is a genuine distance south of here rather than around the corner. Some suppliers will quote a next-day delivery to Port and then explain later why it did not happen. We would rather say at the enquiry that this is a scheduled run, that the realistic window is four to seven business days, and that it is worth telling us your date at the start so we can put you on the right truck rather than the next one.

The practical upside of running it that way is that the delivery is planned rather than improvised. We know before the truck leaves whether your block is sand, backswamp or a slab, whether there is a village window to land inside, whether it is a crane job, and what materials need to be on board for levelling. That is the difference between a container going where you want it on the first attempt and a driver ringing you from the kerb. If your timing is genuinely fixed, a settlement, a site start, a removalist already booked, say so at the enquiry and we will schedule to it instead of explaining afterwards.

sections.h: Sand in front, swamp behind
p: There is a reason we ask which street rather than which suburb. On the beach side the ground is dune sand, which carries very little and lets a concentrated corner load sink unevenly within a season. Behind the dunes the ground is low backswamp that holds water well below a dry-looking surface and does exactly the same thing for the opposite reason. Both end with a frame out of square and doors that need a shoulder, which is the complaint we hear about badly placed units everywhere on this coast.

The answer for both is the same and it is cheap. Concrete pads or hardwood sleepers under the four corner castings, bedded and checked level in both directions and on both diagonals, so the point load spreads over a proper footprint. Get the floor a hundred to a hundred and fifty millimetres clear of the ground so air moves underneath and the bearers are not sitting against damp for a decade, which counts for more here than inland because the water table is shallow. And if your plan involves excavating rather than sitting it on pads, check the acid sulfate soil position with the council first, because a lot of the low country around the Hastings and the Camden Haven is mapped for it.

sections.h: Villages, covenants and the estate rulebook
p: Port Macquarie has a very large retirement and lifestyle village population and a fast-growing set of covenanted estates, and between them they generate more delivery conditions than anywhere else on this coast. In a village, expect the manager to want written notice, a nominated time window, insurance details from the transport operator and a route that avoids a height-limited entry or a driveway they know will not carry weight. In a covenanted estate, expect rules about what may be stored on a lot, whether it can be seen from the road and whether anything may sit forward of the building line.

We will not guess at the rule that applies to your address, because it varies and it is yours to check before you order. What we can say is that the questions are always the same: how long is it staying, can it be seen from the street, is it storage or a conversion, and does a covenant or a body corporate have a say. It is also worth asking what size will be accepted before you decide on one, since plenty of villages and estates will approve a 10ft or 20ft in a nominated spot and will not consider a 40ft anywhere. Get the approval and the window first, then ring us and we will book a truck to land inside it.

faqs.q: Why is delivery to Port Macquarie slower than to Coffs or Grafton?
faqs.a: Because the stock is held at our Grafton depot and Port is a solid run south of it, so we work this stretch of coast as a scheduled run rather than an on-demand one. Four to seven business days is the honest window. The upside is that the job is planned before the truck leaves, with the right materials on board and any village window or crane requirement already sorted. If you have a hard date, tell us at the enquiry and we will put you on a truck that suits it rather than the next one out.

faqs.q: What goes under a container on a sandy block at Lake Cathie or Bonny Hills?
faqs.a: Concrete pads or hardwood sleepers under the four corner castings, bedded and levelled in both directions. Dune sand drains beautifully and carries almost nothing, so a corner casting dropped straight onto sand or thin turf will settle unevenly and the doors will start binding inside a year. On this coast it is also worth getting the floor properly clear of the ground, because the water table is shallow and a floor sitting against damp sand never dries out underneath. Tell us the ground type when you enquire and we will bring the materials.

faqs.q: Can you deliver up the escarpment toward Comboyne or Byabarra?
faqs.a: Yes, and the road decides the size rather than the block does. Those climbs are steep, narrow and tightly wound with low canopy in stretches, and long private driveways up there often run out of turning space at the top, which matters because a tilt-tray has to line up straight before it unloads. A 20ft goes up comfortably. A 40ft needs the whole approach checked first, and where it will not work, two 20ft placed end to end usually gives you more usable space and a much simpler delivery.

faqs.q: Do I need approval for a container in a Port Macquarie estate or village?
faqs.a: Almost certainly in a village, and very likely in a covenanted estate at Thrumster or Sovereign Hills. Villages typically want written notice, a nominated delivery window, insurance details from the transport operator and an approved route. Estate covenants often restrict what can be visible from the street or placed forward of the building line, and many will accept a 10ft or 20ft but not a 40ft. Check it before you order rather than after, get the window in writing, then ring us and we will schedule the truck to land inside it.
